scope: Theorem 28.1 (Measurable axial coefficient) of the manuscript “Spacetime Penrose inequalities: enclosing area, charge, and rigidity” (preprints/Spacetime-Penrose-inequalities-enclosing-area-charge-and-rigidity-October-5-2026/paper.pdf), one of the manuscripts of result family 260 of openai/math at commit 1581d4cbdd69. The statement is quoted verbatim from the text that pdftotext 24.02.0 (-raw -enc UTF-8) extracts from the PDF (SHA-256 794bf524061c4b36), with whitespace normalised, and was found there under this heading on PDF page 167. Text extraction flattens typeset mathematics (superscripts, subscripts, fractions, large operators, delimiters), so the quote can read differently from the typeset statement and can carry characters with no Unicode meaning; the PDF is authoritative. Finding the quote shows that the manuscript states it, not that it is true. AMVO has checked nothing about this claim.
statement: Let U be a four-dimensional coordinate ball B2, or a half-ball B+ 2 = B2 ∩ {x4 > 0}. Assume that the metric is smooth, C−1 g Id ≤ (gij) ≤ Cg Id, and that its coordinate C2 norm is at most Cg. Assume also uniformly bounded C3 norms for the charts and inverse charts. On a half-ball use boundary normal coordinates, so g44 = 1 and ga4 = 0 for a < 4. Let z be C3, up to the flat face when present, and constant on that face. Suppose, almost everywhere, that (28.1) Az : Hessg z = G, Az = Id −(1 − e χ)ez ⊗ ez, ez = grad z | grad z| , 0 < χ0 ≤ e χ ≤ 1. Here e χ and G are measurable. At grad z = 0, any measurable unit axis making the equation true is allowed. If | grad z| ≤ M1 and |G| ≤ N1, then there are α ∈ (0, 1), r0 > 0 and C < ∞ such that (28.2) ∥ grad z∥Cα(U1) ≤ C(M1 + N1), Z Br(x)∩U | Hessg z|2 dVg ≤ C(M1 + N1)2 r2+2α for x ∈ U1 and 0 < r ≤ r0, where U1 = B1 or B+ 1 . The constants depend only on χ0, the stated geometry bounds and the separation from the curved patch edges. The Cα norm may equivalently be taken for the coordinate gradient components. In particular, no modulus of continuity of G or e χ, and no bound for a derivative of either, is assumed.
